# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

## Lead

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a long-track, violent EF3 tornado that struck Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties in west-central Alabama on April 27, 2011, during the 2011 Super Outbreak of tornadoes across the southern United States. The tornado developed in far southwestern Greene County near the Tombigbee River and tracked northeast for about 72 miles, reaching a maximum width of approximately 1 mile (1760 yards) before dissipating near Marvel in northeastern Bibb County. Along its path through rural communities including Tishabee, Sawyerville, and Eoline, the tornado produced severe structural damage to mobile homes, single-family residences, churches, businesses, and the Eoline Fire Department, while downing thousands of trees. In total, the event caused approximately 7 fatalities and 50 injuries, with most of the deaths and injuries occurring in Hale County near Sawyerville and an additional fatality and injuries near Eoline. Tornado warnings were in effect for the affected counties as the storm moved through, but the intensity and breadth of the damage made the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado one of the more destructive individual tornadoes associated with the late April 2011 outbreak in Alabama. [1][17][7][16][15][8][10]

## Background and meteorological setting

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred on April 27, 2011, a day when an exceptionally strong storm system produced a widespread and deadly tornado outbreak across the southeastern United States. According to the National Severe Storms Laboratory, more than 200 tornadoes were recorded between April 25 and 28, 2011, with 122 tornadoes and 319 fatalities occurring on April 27 alone, making it one of the deadliest tornado days in the United States since modern records began in 1950. The broader outbreak, often termed the 2011 Super Outbreak, was characterized by a deep surface low-pressure system over the central United States, strong wind shear through the lower and middle troposphere, and very unstable air over the Southeast, which together supported numerous tornadic supercells. [16]

Regional retrospective accounts describe multiple supercells tracking across Alabama on April 27, producing several significant tornadoes including the Sawyerville–Eoline event. A narrative produced using geospatial reconstructions of the outbreak notes that a tornado moved through portions of the Talladega National Forest in Hale and Bibb counties, corresponding to the path of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as documented by local National Weather Service surveys. These retrospective sources focus on the overall outbreak rather than detailed mesoscale analyses of the parent storm, and available public documents do not specify the exact convective mode or storm-scale evolution of the individual supercell responsible for the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado. [8][10][11][1]

Government and academic climatological work examining the April 2011 tornadoes place the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado within a larger pattern of numerous strong and violent tornadoes interacting with populated areas, contributing to high casualty totals in Alabama and neighboring states. However, these technical studies emphasize aggregate statistics and physical properties of many tornadoes rather than providing storm-specific synoptic or mesoscale diagnoses for the Sawyerville–Eoline case, leaving some details of the precise meteorological evolution of this tornado undocumented in publicly accessible sources. [5][6][10][16]

## Tornado chronology and path

National Weather Service Birmingham event documentation indicates that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado touched down in far southwestern Greene County near the Tombigbee River, just west of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, before moving northeast across rural portions of the county north of Forkland. In this segment, the tornado initially produced EF1 damage and then strengthened to EF2 intensity, damaging or destroying at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches, and downing numerous trees; two minor injuries were reported in Greene County. [1]

From Greene County, the tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and entered Hale County west of Sawyerville, then crossed Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, where survey teams found damage indicative of EF3 intensity with estimated winds of about 145 mph. The National Centers for Environmental Information Storm Events Database lists the Hale County portion of the tornado as an EF3 event with a path length of roughly 25.18 miles and a maximum width of 1760 yards, beginning near a point approximately 4.9 miles west of Sawyerville and ending near a point about 3.6 miles east-southeast of Phipps. [1][17]

As the tornado progressed through Hale County, it crossed County Roads 18 and 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram, producing extensive structural damage and downing thousands of trees along its path. The storm then moved into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, causing significant tree damage up to the Bibb County line, consistent with accounts that a tornado traversed forested areas of Hale and Bibb counties during the outbreak. [1][17][8]

Entering Bibb County near Eoline, the tornado maintained EF3 intensity with estimated winds around 145 mph, causing minor to major damage to numerous mobile homes and single-family residences and destroying about a dozen such structures along with the Eoline Fire Department and another business. After passing through Eoline, the tornado weakened slightly to EF2 strength with estimated winds of about 125 mph as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, where several mobile and single-family homes near County Road 26 sustained major damage or were destroyed. The tornado continued to weaken as it tracked northeast, finally lifting just northeast of Marvel in Bibb County. [1]

Across all three counties, the combined damage path of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was estimated at approximately 72.13 miles long, with a maximum width of about 1760 yards (around 1 mile), as summarized in the Birmingham office’s event page and corroborated in outbreak retrospectives. The Alabama Tornadoes 2011 database compiled by the National Weather Service lists an entry for the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado among 146 tornado occurrences documented in the state for 2011, providing tabular confirmation of its EF3 rating, path length, width, and casualty totals. [1][7][15]

## Damage and casualties

Throughout Greene County, damage associated with the initial portion of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was primarily classified as EF1 to EF2, with survey reports documenting at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches damaged or destroyed, along with widespread tree damage. Two minor injuries were reported within Greene County, and event summaries do not indicate fatalities in this segment of the path. [1][17]

In Hale County, the tornado caused the majority of the event’s casualties and structural damage, with National Weather Service and Storm Events Database entries reporting 6 direct fatalities and at least 40 injuries within this portion of the path. Extensive structural damage occurred along routes including County Roads 18 and 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram, where numerous mobile homes, single-family residences, and at least one church were damaged or destroyed. Property damage for the Hale County segment was estimated at approximately US$17 million, with no crop damage reported. [1][17]

Near Sawyerville, observers and survey teams described “extensive structural damage”, with many mobile homes and wood-frame houses severely damaged or demolished and debris scattered widely, consistent with EF3 intensity and estimated 145 mph winds. Thousands of trees were snapped or uprooted across this area, contributing to blocked roads and complicating immediate emergency access following the tornado. Retrospective outbreak coverage by regional media reiterates that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was among the more damaging west-central Alabama tornadoes on April 27, citing its long track and severe impacts to housing stock in low-density rural communities. [1][17][7][11]

In Bibb County near Eoline, the tornado maintained EF3 intensity for part of its track, causing minor to major damage to numerous mobile homes and single-family residences and destroying about a dozen such structures. The Eoline Fire Department building and another business were destroyed, and one person was killed in a vehicle near the fire department, with at least ten other injuries recorded in the Eoline area. As the tornado weakened to EF2 while crossing Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, several additional mobile and single-family homes near County Road 26 sustained major damage or were destroyed, and damage surveys noted thousands of trees downed along the remainder of the path toward Marvel. [1]

Summarizing the entire event, National Weather Service and outbreak retrospectives report that the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado caused approximately 7 fatalities and 50 injuries across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties combined. Most of the deaths and injuries occurred in Hale County near Sawyerville, where six fatalities and around forty injuries were documented, while one additional fatality and multiple injuries occurred near Eoline in Bibb County. Publicly available sources do not provide a detailed breakdown of injuries by community beyond these county-level figures. [1][7][17]

## Aftermath and legacy

Tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from roughly 4:50 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. local time on April 27, 2011, covering the period during which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado tracked across the region. National Weather Service Birmingham documentation notes that forecasters issued warnings for the affected counties well before the tornado reached Sawyerville and Eoline, reflecting heightened situational awareness during the broader outbreak day. However, the combination of a long-track, strong tornado and the presence of vulnerable structures such as mobile homes meant that significant casualties still occurred despite the warning lead time. [1][16][6]

Outbreak retrospectives produced by AL.com and other regional outlets describe extensive emergency response and recovery operations across Alabama following the April 27 tornadoes, including search-and-rescue efforts, provision of temporary shelter, and long-term rebuilding in impacted communities such as Sawyerville and Eoline. These accounts emphasize the cumulative burden of dozens of tornado tracks intersecting both urban areas, such as Tuscaloosa and Birmingham, and rural communities, which strained local emergency management resources and led to state and federal disaster declarations. Specific, detailed narratives of the post-event recovery process in Sawyerville and Eoline are limited in broadly accessible sources, with most documentation focusing on casualty statistics and structural damage rather than long-term social or economic impacts. [7][8][11][1]

In the months following the outbreak, the Alabama Department of Public Health and other agencies produced newsletters and assessments highlighting the scale of emergency medical services deployment and emphasizing preparedness and coordination lessons from the April 2011 tornadoes. These documents reference the April 27 tornado impacts, including those in Hale and Bibb counties, in the context of statewide emergency response performance and do not isolate the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as a separate case study, suggesting that its legacy in official discourse is closely tied to the broader outbreak rather than treated as a standalone disaster. [12][7][10]

Academic work on tornado casualties and kinetic energy has used data from the 2011 Super Outbreak, including events in Alabama, to explore relationships between tornado characteristics, exposure, and casualty outcomes. These studies incorporate the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as part of aggregated datasets, illustrating that strong, long-track tornadoes intersecting rural housing composed largely of mobile homes can still produce high casualty counts despite modern warning systems. While such research does not focus on the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado individually, it contributes to the broader understanding of why tornadoes of this type remain deadly and informs mitigation and preparedness discussions in Alabama and other tornado-prone regions. [5][6][16]

## Context within the April 2011 Alabama tornado outbreak

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed part of the April 27, 2011 sequence of tornadoes that severely impacted Alabama, including high-profile events in Tuscaloosa-Birmingham, Cullman, Hackleburg–Phil Campbell, and other communities. Retrospective outbreak narratives and timelines list the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as an EF3 event occurring around 5:30 p.m. with estimated winds of 145 mph, affecting Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties and producing seven deaths and fifty injuries along a 72.13-mile track. These accounts categorize the tornado among the strong, long-track tornadoes that contributed significantly to Alabama’s April 27 casualty total, though they generally emphasize the overall outbreak impact rather than presenting detailed rankings of individual tornadoes by intensity or fatalities. [7][10][11][16]

Within statewide compilations of 2011 tornadoes, the Alabama Tornadoes 2011 database produced by the National Weather Service Birmingham office lists 146 tornado occurrences in Alabama during that year, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado as a significant EF3 event. This database provides standardized information on each tornado—such as EF rating, path length and width, and casualty counts—and demonstrates that the April 27 outbreak contained a concentration of strong and violent tornadoes relative to the rest of 2011 in Alabama. Publicly available summaries refrain from assigning ordinal rankings or superlatives to the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado beyond noting its casualty toll and long path within the broader outbreak context. [15][10][16][7]

## Conflict in reported timing

There is a documented discrepancy in publicly available sources regarding the timing of the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado’s onset. The National Weather Service Birmingham event summary describes the overall tornado path as beginning around 5:30 p.m. local time and ending around 6:55 p.m., consistent with its long-track progression across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties. In contrast, a statewide emergency medical services newsletter from the Alabama Department of Public Health discusses the April 27 tornado impacts using a wider time window of approximately 5:30 p.m. to 6:55 p.m. for the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, which may reflect the period during which EMS activity or impacts were recorded rather than the precise meteorological onset. These differences indicate that operational and retrospective sources may define event timing based on slightly different criteria, and available documentation does not fully reconcile these approaches. [1][12][14]
